questions.q: State the SI unit of the energy equivalent of 1 kg of mass according to \(E = mc^2\), and write the numerical value of \(c\) to be used in calculations.
questions.a: The SI unit is joule (J). The speed of light \(c = 3.00 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s}\) (approximate) or \(2.9979 \times 10^8 \, \text{m/s}\) (exact). A wrong answer like "MeV" or "eV" reveals confusion between SI units and nuclear physics convenience units; a wrong value of \(c\) (e.g., \(3 \times 10^5 \, \text{km/s}\) without conversion) reveals unit inconsistency.

questions.q: A student writes: "In a chemical reaction like burning coal, mass is conserved exactly, so \(E = mc^2\) does not apply." Explain why this statement is incorrect, and estimate the order of magnitude of the mass defect for a reaction releasing 1 eV of energy.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect because \(E = mc^2\) applies universally; mass-energy interconversion occurs in chemical reactions too, but the mass defect is ~\(10^{-9}\) u (since 1 eV = \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) J → \(\Delta m = E/c^2 \approx 1.78 \times 10^{-36}\) kg ≈ \(10^{-9}\) u), which is too small to measure. A student who thinks mass is strictly conserved in chemistry has not grasped that mass defect exists but is negligible compared to nuclear reactions (where defects are ~0.1 u per nucleon).

questions.q: Calculate the energy equivalent (in MeV) of the mass defect \(\Delta m = 0.13691 \, \text{u}\) for the \(^{16}_8\text{O}\) nucleus, using \(1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV}/c^2\). Show unit cancellation explicitly.
questions.a: \(E = \Delta m \times 931.5 \, \text{MeV}/c^2 \times c^2 = 0.13691 \times 931.5 \, \text{MeV} = 127.5 \, \text{MeV}\). Steps: (1) Identify \(\Delta m = 0.13691 \, \text{u}\). (2) Use conversion \(1 \, \text{u} = 931.5 \, \text{MeV}/c^2\). (3) Multiply: \(0.13691 \times 931.5 = 127.5\). (4) Units: u × (MeV/c²)/u × c² = MeV. A wrong answer like 127.5 J or forgetting \(c^2\) cancellation reveals unit-tracking failure.

questions.q: Two nuclei, \(^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}\) and \(^{238}_{92}\text{U}\), have binding energies per nucleon of 8.75 MeV and 7.6 MeV respectively. Which nucleus is more tightly bound? If \(^{238}\text{U}\) splits into two \(^{119}\) fragments each with 8.5 MeV/nucleon, estimate the total energy released. Explain the physical reasoning.
questions.a: \(^{56}\text{Fe}\) is more tightly bound (higher \(E_b/A\)). For fission: initial total binding energy = \(238 \times 7.6 = 1808.8 \, \text{MeV}\). Final total binding energy = \(2 \times 119 \times 8.5 = 2023 \, \text{MeV}\). Energy released = \(2023 - 1808.8 = 214.2 \, \text{MeV}\). The reasoning: energy is released when less bound nucleons reorganize into more bound configurations; the mass defect increases, so mass decreases, and the difference appears as kinetic energy of fragments. A student who subtracts per-nucleon values (8.5 – 7.6 = 0.9 MeV) and multiplies by 238 gets the same number but must justify why multiplication by total nucleons is correct.

questions.q: A proposed "perpetual motion" machine claims to convert 1 g of water completely into energy continuously without any mass input. Evaluate this claim using \(E = mc^2\) and the law of conservation of mass-energy. What fundamental principle does it violate?
questions.a: The claim violates conservation of mass-energy. Converting 1 g of water yields \(E = (10^{-3} \, \text{kg})(3 \times 10^8)^2 = 9 \times 10^{13} \, \text{J}\) once. After that, the mass is gone; you cannot get more energy without new mass input. The machine would need a source of mass to sustain output. A student who says "it violates energy conservation" is partially correct but misses the unified mass-energy conservation: mass is the fuel, and it is consumed.

questions.q: Design a simple thought experiment to demonstrate that the binding energy of a nucleus must be included in its total mass. Use a system of two protons and two neutrons combining to form \(^4_2\text{He}\). Specify initial and final masses, and the energy released.
questions.a: Initial: 2 free protons (2 × 1.00727 u) + 2 free neutrons (2 × 1.00866 u) = 4.03186 u. Final: \(^4_2\text{He}\) nucleus (atomic mass 4.002603 u minus 2 electron masses 2×0.000548 u = 4.001507 u). Mass defect = 0.030353 u. Energy released = 0.030353 × 931.5 MeV = 28.27 MeV. The helium nucleus is lighter by exactly this mass equivalent. A poor answer omits electron mass subtraction or uses atomic masses directly without adjustment, showing confusion between atomic and nuclear masses.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: This means mass is a concentrated form of energy, and any change in the total energy of a closed system results in a ______ change in its mass.
Fill in the blank: Observe a nuclear reactor or the Sun: both release ______ energy from tiny amounts of matter.
